roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Can I ask  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Would you  -- I mean, would you  --and just to follow up on what Justice Jackson is asking, do you think we can  read (b)(5)(A) at least to say we're ruling out APA review here?
Your Honor, I don't want to belabor that point because our brief addresses it at great length.

In our view, there is a difference from the Department of Commerce case between whether the record evidence supports the conclusion and whether the decision is motivated by some impermissible criteria.
And in Department of Commerce, obviously, the record evidence did support the conclusion, but nonetheless, the decision was based on, you know, a contrived reason.
That  is the reason why we think pretext claims are reviewable.
But it doesn't matter because the first two claims are  --are much more canonically sort of old -- you know, older than SEC v. Chenery.
You know, I think that decision really becomes reviewable.

This becomes canonical APA law that pretext claims should be understood differently after Chenery  I, but these other ideas are much, much older than that, and that's really, you know, all we  have to say about it.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, in Department of Commerce, of course, we said that political considerations are a permissible factor.
How are we supposed to determine how much political influence is too much?
Yeah.
I  --I think, in this case, the Secretary said on CNN the day after her first TPS decision that we are taking direction from the direction of the President, he is pausing this program.
And after that -- meaning the TPS program.
And then there have been 13 terminations in a row.
So the district court just said on -- we're here on preliminary relief.

I think it's a factual finding for clear error review. The  -- the district court said, you know, I think that I will take that statement, when  coupled with the confirmatory action of all the TPS terminations and the absence of consultation and all the rest of it, to mean that  --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, that's a particular circumstance.
But, I mean, in  general, how would you articulate the principle that this is too much?  How do you judge, as a general matter, how much political influence is too much?
Only --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Not  -- not that you're saying, well, it was too much in this case but more generally.
Yeah.
I mean, I don't think -- I wouldn't change a word of Commerce, Your Honor, and --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I wouldn't either.
(Laughter.)
Yes.
I figured you would say that.

And  --and I just  --I just think this is also a very rare outlier case where the Secretary actually said on national television the day after the decision that she  was motivated by an impermissible factor.
You know, I want to come back to this consultation question, though, to talk about this email.
As Justice Sotomayor had said, the  entire consultation in this case is reprinted on less than one page, page 41 of our brief.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, could I ask about that particularly?  Suppose that there  was the same question asked from DHS to State Department, and instead of the answer being State has no foreign policy concerns with ending these TPS designations, suppose the answer was just State has no concerns with  ending these TPS designations.
I mean  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Would that be appropriate?  Would that be  -- would that cross the line into that's fine?

I mean, that is a much harder case than ours because it might be true that no concerns encompasses country conditions, you know, and I'm not saying that definitely that person should win because I think, you know, you  --the -- the government -- I mean the plaintiffs may be entitled to -- to -- to argue that that's not actually what happened there.
But our case is so much easier than that because  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, is it so much easier?  I mean, I wonder -- I mean, the State  Department probably says no foreign policy concerns five times before breakfast every day. It's just  -- it's --that's what the  -- the State Department.
They deal with foreign policy concerns.
So, if somebody asks them something, they say no foreign policy concerns.

Does that really -- is that really going to make the difference between what is permissible consultation and what is not permissible consultation, the fact that they  put the words "foreign policy" in the answer?
So  -- so two things.

First, this same exact worded email, no foreign policy concerns or sometimes they  said foreign policy objections, but foreign policy concerns or objections is now the record in seven consecutive TPS terminations under this statute.
And that's why all these  district courts that they're talking about, right, it's the same thing.
So it's not obvious to me that, oh, they could have just written country conditions and they chose to write foreign policy.
You know, but, you know, I'd still say turn the  square corner and make them -- make them do it.
But, beyond that, there is  -- you know, we  -- we have also our --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: When you say that, when you say, look, this is -- this is obviously deliberate language because it was used in seven, what are you suggesting about why they used this language?

So, look, I -- I don't -- I don't know, but I think it is  possible that they don't have a foreign policy concern, but they're not comfortable saying that the armed conflict in Syria is over when their own website is saying, if you go to Syria, leave a DNA sample, execute a will before you go, it's active armed conflict, no  part of Syria is safe, every part is wracked with violence  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, it's not the Assad regime anymore, though.
I mean, that -- the whole thing was the Assad regime after 53 years of complete oppression and brutal treatment is gone.
But  --so, Your Honor --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So do you agree the Assad regime change is a significant change in the history of that country and the -- and the Middle East more broadly?
I mean, of course, anybody would agree with that, Your Honor, but I  -- but --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.

Well, that's an important marker then because that's -- that's a -- a big shift in both Syria  but also the posture of other countries towards Syria, at least as I  --I don't pretend to be an expert, but that's my understanding of what's the backdrop here.
So  -- so two thoughts, Your Honor.
Then I want to briefly talk about national interest if  --if there's time.

So, first, you know, we're not -- we're not interested in a debate about whether Syria is or is not safe, so, you know, we haven't gotten into that precisely because it's barred by the judicial review bar, right?  Our  view is they have to consult and that's the end of it.

And the second thing I would say is the State Department's own reports believe, of course, Assad  --they recognize Assad has ended, but they say active violence in every  part of the country, the daycare that Laila Doe's daughter went to got bombed, the building next to it has been bombed again in southern Syria.
That's not the same conflict.
It's the Israeli incursion.
There's a war between Turkey and Kurdistan  --Kurds going on in the north.
There's still lots of conflict  according to the State Department's accounts and the  --the CRS report about this.
These are in the Joint Appendix.
So I don't think it's as simple as that, but we don't contest, if the Secretary says, I disagree, Syria is safe, that's fine, but she still has to turn the square corners and follow the steps.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.
Justice Thomas, anything further?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Just briefly with respect to the jurisdiction-stripping provision again.
If the Secretary actually designates  -- does not terminate but designates in favor of  -- of a particular group, can others use the exact same objection that you're offering?
I'm not sure I understand the question, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, would they be able to challenge the same way that you're challenging --
I got it.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- a positive designation?
Got it.
So, no, Your Honor, but not because of the review bar. What they can challenge -- the statute says the Secretary may designate  -- this is -- now we're talking about (b)(1), right?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, yeah.
May designate only if, and then one of these three criteria have to be met.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.
So, even if a country is horribly in crisis, there's no obligation to designate.
And that's the reason why that's unreviewable, you know.

But, of course, it doesn't cut the other way, right?  On their view, if the Secretary  --this was my opening hypothetical  -- if the Secretary designated Mexico for immigration relief, it's unreviewable.
On our view, it is reviewable  because you look to the -- to the criteria to see whether they actually applied.
Did they care at all about conditions, or were they just  trying to achieve some political end?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Alito?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: One of the points that General Sauer made was that if we accept your arguments, it will create a hole in the  judicial review bar that you could drive a convoy of trucks through.

And you have now said repeatedly that it's necessary for the Secretary to turn square corners, which seems to open  --which seems to support what he says, that if we depart from  the ordinary meaning of the review bar, then it is always going to be possible to pick procedural faults in  --to raise procedural objections to what's been done.
And what you've said about consultation makes me think that that may be true because, here, there was some consultation.

All right, it was very brief  and maybe it's not what one would hope for, but still, once you say, well, it's -- it's permissible to review the adequacy of the  --of the consultation, it's always going to be possible to pick -- to -- to raise objections about the adequacy of the -- of the consultation and the words that the State Department comes back with.
So two thoughts, Your Honor.
First, our consultation claim in this sense is extremely narrow.
We don't argue about the levels.
We don't argue about the amount.
All we say is it has to be about a subject, deliberation about a subject, so they  have to talk about country conditions.

And you could hold that, Your Honor, and leave aside, just say we're not saying it's  okay to police meaningfulness, even though, in other statutes, lower courts do  --you know, consultation claims  -- consultation provisions are in other  -- other statutes and, you know, the sky doesn't fall.
But, if  -- if your -- that's Your Honor's concern, just only say it has to be about the topic, and  --and we don't say anything about, you know, meaningfulness in a broader sense.
That's my first answer.
My second answer is, you know, the State Department actually provided reports  because they did care about speaking in one voice for 35 years under this statute.

This is  in the former senior government officials' brief, a bipartisan brief, including somebody from the first Trump administration talking about the fact that they used to actually look  at all the different components of the State Department and talk about this so that they could make sure that the decision was good.
There was never a challenge to consultation under that.
Even in the first Trump administration  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You think that sort of elaborate process is necessary --
No.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- under this statute?
No.
No, I do not, Your Honor, I do not.
My point is just, you know, it wasn't a problem until the form emails started.

Even in the first Trump administration, when there were  --that was the first time there were other TPS challenges. Before that, 16 designations  --terminations, never a challenge, right?  It started then.
Even after that, this consultation claim has only arisen because now they're doing the form email.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Sotomayor?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Barrett sort of was asking a question about -- almost sounded a little bit like harmless error, even if they didn't consult.
That's okay because, you know, they were going to make the same decision.
How do you deal with that?  I mean, this is a due process claim, and we've never said what the final  determination is important to due process, correct?
Yeah, correct, Your Honor.
You know, I think I would say two things about it.

First, there isn't a basis in  this record to say that she would have done the same thing if the State  --particularly on the armed conflict designation, where national  interest is not a criteria, so you have to find that  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's under the (A)  section of the statute?
Correct, it's under (b)(1)(A).
That's  --there's two designations for Syria, one under armed conflict and the other under extraordinary temporary conditions.

Our position is that even under the latter one, it is not permissible to consider national interest at the periodic review stage because what is required is that there be review of conditions in the foreign state.
And we think, when the word "conditions" is used, you know, just a couple lines later, it's referring back to conditions  in the foreign state and not criteria, which is what my friend kept saying.
And if you look at the  -- the word, the name, the label of it is extraordinary and temporary conditions, which is talking about country conditions; (b)(1)(B)  also says living conditions.
So every time the word "conditions" is used in  -- in subsection (b), it's talking about country conditions.
National interest is not a condition, right?  So that -- that's our  --our argument, our  --our argument on the merits as to the second one.
But, on the first one, even as to process, there's nothing in this record to tell you that if they had actually consulted, the Secretary would have said, I don't care what the State Department says.
Maybe she would have said, oh, wow, that's not good.
And they would have perhaps, you know, led to a different view.

And so I think, even if harmless error is permissible in this context, there just isn't a basis to find it, and it -- it is again important for the government to speak in one voice, and I think that would be the benefit of  -- of imposing -- enforcing the consultation requirement here.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, I mean, the whole purpose of -- of the TPS is to ensure  that the executive is open about what it's doing, correct?
Yes, Your Honor. Transparency is all through the statute, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And so, to the extent that a President says country -- it's not safe for these people to come back or I'm unwilling to say it's safe for those people to come back, Haiti shows that four of the people who were sent back, that have gone back, were killed.
So I -- I'm not going to say it, but I don't care, I'm still going to end the program,  that that's a different impact than saying it's safe  --
It  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- and I have an alternative reason anyway?
It absolutely is, Your Honor.

And I think it's also important to remember that this issue about whether you can terminate on the basis of national interest, it only arises if the country is still unsafe, the alternative ground, right, it only arises if the country is still unsafe and as to people who have been able to keep their TPS because  despite being vetted 18 months, every 18 months, resubmitting their background, resubmitting criminal history checks, they have  been found not to have even a single felony or more than one misdemeanor or any of the other grounds.
So we're talking about the power to  mass expel people who have done nothing wrong to countries that remain unsafe.
And our view is it is unlikely that a refugee protection statute would have given that power to the Secretary.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What do you do with  --there are two pools here.
One is the people who have been given TPS status for a long period of time and the new applicants for which there hasn't been checking yet.
Yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Could a President come and say the problem -- I'm not going to terminate the program because the country's  still not safe, but I'm not going to give new applicants permission to stay because I can't vet those guys?
Yes, absolutely, Your Honor.
So, in the periodic review  process, there's three options.
You can  terminate, you can extend, and if you extend, you can also designate -- designate again, but you don't have to.
If you designate again, that updates the date and has the effect of then bringing new people into the eligibility criteria.
But  the statute doesn't mandate that.
It mandates extension if the country is unsafe, but it does not mandate designation.
That is like a new designation.

And so, absolutely, the government could take the position either individually or  categorically that we're not going to do any new designations, no more TPS holders, but this fixed population, the people who already have it and have come to rely on the fact that if the government is  -- determines that their country is unsafe, then they get to stay, they would still -- that closed population would still be protected, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So that answers the General's position about this being a pull country in some way, that our policy is a pull?
Yes, Your Honor.
I think my  --my friend for the Miot plaintiffs will also point out that there's no evidence for this  -- this claim about the pull factor. I'll leave that to them, but yes, Your Honor  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: There are --
-- there is no need, you can  --you can just solve the problem by saying we're not going to let any new people into the program.
We are going to limit our extensions to countries that are unsafe for people who already have TPS.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The people who are here, however, and previously been vetted, no  -- there's no new problem with that vetting for them?
No, Your Honor.
In fact, the  --the statute requires that their TPS be rescinded if they commit a felony or become inadmissible on any of a very broad set of grounds.
So it's  -- it's extremely narrow protection.
But, if they -- if they don't, if they do nothing wrong, then  -- and their country is still unsafe, the statute requires that they remain protected.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kagan?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Your argument that the national interest claim is reviewable seems harder to me than the procedural argument, and here's why.

I mean, I would have thought it's a  -- it's just a -- a version of an argument that is made all the time when it comes to administrative action, like you took the wrong factors into account or, you know, you didn't take the right factors into account.
That's a  kind of standard part of arbitrary and capricious review.
And I would have thought that if this judicial review provision does anything, it basically says don't subject the Secretary's determination to arbitrary -and -capricious review as we know it.
Mm-hmm.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So why should we treat this argument, this national interest argument, any differently?

So I think there's some categorical distinction in my head between an argument like, oh, you looked at the earthquake recovery in this portion of the  country but not in that portion of the country or you didn't consider this evidence about how the armed conflict is in the southern part but not the eastern part.

Those are still within the purview of the statutory criteria about armed conflict or temporary living conditions, right?  But it's  something else if the Secretary says, oh, I'm designating the  -- I'm terminating the armed conflict designation because there -- there's been earthquake recovery.
But earthquake is not a criteria for the armed conflict.
It's only a criteria under (b)(1)(B).

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, that makes it sound as though, if there's any legal error attached to the Secretary's determination, review can come in.
And is  -- is --is -- are  -- are you reading the review provision that way, that it's just about factual errors, not legal errors?
I -- I do think -- I do think there can be -- I mean, when we're talking about Guerrero -Lasprilla and Wilkinson definition of legal error, obviously, that might be broad.
I don't think the Court has to say that those are reviewable.

But the claim that we're making here is that the national interest, you heard me say it, right, the national interest is only at the  outset, and it's not in the periodic review because periodic review is a conditions analysis whereas national interest is not described as a condition, it's in  contradistinction to conditions.
That is a pure question of law.
You don't need to know anything  -- anything at all about facts in order to assess that criteria question.
And, Your Honor, there  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But it's also very easy for Congress to write a review provision that's confined to non -legal questions.
And that's not what Congress did here.
That's true, Your Honor, although they also can easily say  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean  --
-- all questions --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- this has nothing to do with, like, even if I read this statute as saying determination, is with respect to the  determination about country conditions, but if  -- if you're in that world where the question is, like, how did you determine country conditions, whether you made a factual error, whether you made a legal error, Congress  in this provision seems not to care.
So I agree that this provision doesn't read fact law into it one way or another.

And I  -- I think our narrower argument  -- Justice Alito had said -- you know, I took the question to be maybe -- maybe I'm not buying your full -- full-bore determination argument, do you have anything to fall back?  And what I was saying was, if you  -- if you don't want to take the full textual view, then read it against the backdrop of administrative law, where, obviously, this Court generally or courts generally have the  last view on questions of law.

But I think, if you say no, that's not the  -- what they're doing here, so some legal questions are going to be barred, what I would say is, whether or not this is within the scope of the determination, that is our -- what we  are disputing, right, because we're saying it's  not a country condition because it doesn't use the word "condition" to describe it, and the review provision is limited to conditions in the foreign state.
And this is not in the foreign state.

So, at least that claim, the threshold question of, like, do you get into the  reviewability bar or not, that should be reviewable even if, once we're in it, you would say, like, a legal  -- a --a legal dispute about which kinds of conditions should be in it or not, that that would be barred, you know.

And we don't -- we don't believe that that necessarily is the case either, but just to be clear, like, our claim is, at the very highest level, it's just about the criteria of even what counts as a condition.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Gorsuch?  Justice Kavanaugh?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How many Syrians have returned to Syria since the end of the Assad regime?  And is that of any relevance to  what you've been saying about country conditions?
I mean, I'd say the same thing that I said to you earlier, Your Honor.
Two answers.

First is it is of no  relevance because, even if the Secretary is right and the State Department is wrong, it doesn't change the fact that they didn't talk to each other, and the national interest is not a criteria and those are claims that are clearly reviewable under the statute.
So, A, that's my answer.

Second, it is true that people have  -- many people have gone from Lebanon back into Syria, but if we're  -- if we're reading the newspaper now and sort of outside the administrative record, there might be good reasons why people are going from southern Lebanon back to Syria if they're having to pick between the two places.
And that is not the same thing as saying, oh, we're going from California to Syria.
And so I don't think the fact that you have this mass movement of people is necessarily indicative of whether it is safe to  go there or not.
As I said, there is still active armed conflict.
There's bombing happening now in Syria.
So, you know, it may be better or worse.
Some people say the mortality rate is higher.
I haven't  -- you know, I don't know.
But, anyway, yeah, that -- I think -- I think it does not answer the question ultimately, even though  -- even if it did, we still should win.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Barrett?  Justice Jackson?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So I'm interested in the standards applicable to our decision-making in this case, and one of them is the thought that even if "determination" could be read to mean different things, the final conclusion or  close to it, versus the final conclusion plus the antecedent steps, I thought we had a  presumption of reviewability that was supposed to apply to our interpretive analysis in a situation like this.
So am I wrong about that?
You're absolutely right, Your Honor.
It's applied in Bowen, in  McNary, in Catholic Social Services, and, of course, in Guerrero-Lasprilla, you know, and -- and Wilkinson.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So, when Justice Thomas says, well, the background is that we wouldn't interpret this in -- if we're sort of trying to figure out what "determination" is, we  -- we -- we wouldn't allow for you to review it, I think the opposite is true.

In other words, if there's some confusion about the express  -- the scope of the express determination -- the express review  bar, I thought our rules under our precedents say you're supposed to interpret it narrowly.
Yes, Your Honor. Two things on this.
First, the presumption is clear that they have to show clear and convincing evidence.

So the question is, you  know, is what we've said by hooking it to "determine" or read it against the hundred years of administrative law good enough to just  get above what would be needed, you know, to beat clear and convincing.
And I think it is.

And the second thing I'd say on that subject is, Your Honor, Biden v. Texas from  just a couple years ago, this Court holds the APA governs the DHS's parole policy, and it has to be reasonable and reasonably explained against  --and they  --it reaches that holding, every judge -- justice of this Court endorses  that idea in the face of a jurisdiction-stripping argument which the government makes about the scope of the injunction and, you know, all of that I'm sure you all remember.

And so it's both true that, as a general matter, this Court has applied the presumption in both large and small immigration  cases and also that it has done it particularly in a context like this one, where the issue is about whether Mexico, you know, basically, the  --had to be -- the U.S. had to be forced to negotiate with Mexico.
And so --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.

And my second -- my second issue about standards, is  there a clear error standard that is applicable to the district court's findings here, findings  of fact, for example, about whether or not there was likely discriminatory intent with respect to this policy?
Yes, absolutely, Your Honor.

It is both true  --it's double deference, I would argue, because it's both  here on preliminary relief, there may be more evidence to come if the case is allowed to survive, certainly, the constitutional claim is going to be allowed to survive given the -- on jurisdiction anyway, and, in addition, because  factual findings are reviewed for clear error in general, then it is true that -- that clear error operates there.
I think that now, since we have the email about consultation and we all agree that that's the scope of it, it's not really relevant.
You can read that one page of our brief --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Or it's just so obviously not an error, not a clear error as a result of that evidence, right?
Well, yes, Your Honor, absolutely.
I mean  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean, we're still applying the clear error -- you're not saying jettison the clear error standard; you're just saying look at this evidence.

If the district court found it to be that the email in terms of  consultation or the discriminatory intent in terms of what the President said -- our -- our burden is to determine whether or not she made a clear error in her fact-finding related to those issues, correct?
Yes, absolutely, Your Honor.

And the last thing I would just say about that is, on the pretext claim, where I know there  -- maybe everybody doesn't think that we have all the evidence, it's not the evidence that was in Commerce because it was a full trial in Commerce.
I think, in that  context too, it is relevant that we are here on preliminary relief because the district court was looking at it and that's  --that's what you've got.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.
Mr. Pipoly.
Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  For decades, administrations of both parties successfully terminated TPS designations without inviting litigation.
They  did so by following the process Congress set forth in the TPS statute.
The termination of Haiti's TPS was different.
It was not the result of the mandatory review process but was instead a preordained result driven by the President's resolve to end TPS for Haiti no matter what.
The reasons Secretary Noem gave for the termination were pretextual.
The DHS documents that we already lodged with this Court show that the Secretary's purported review was a sham.
Agency staff was "forced" to include rationales for termination that had no empirical support.
The true reason for the termination of the  --for the termination is the President's racial animus towards non-white immigrants and bare dislike of Haitians in particular.

The  President has disparaged Haitian TPS holders specifically as undesirables from a "shithole country," and days after falsely accusing them of "eating the dogs and eating the cats of Americans," he vowed that he would terminate  Haiti's TPS, and that is exactly what happened.
Recognizing all this, the district court correctly postponed the termination. This Court should affirm.
And I welcome the Court's questions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What weight do you  -- how would you interpret the jurisdiction-stripping provision?
No different than the Doe plaintiffs do, Justice Thomas.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: More generally, is there anything that your friend  said that you disagree with?
No, Justice -- Chief Justice  --Mr. Chief Justice.
My apologies.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Whatever. (Laughter.)

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Can I ask about your equal protection claim?
Certainly.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Is this -- is this a  -- a race claim or is it a national origin claim, or does it matter?

It's  -- it's --it's a -- it's certainly a race-based claim, we would argue, given the -- as -- as some of the questioning earlier got to, the evidence certainly suggests racial animus, which, under -- which  --which the Arlington Heights framework is specifically designed to suss out.

The -- the statements, "I would like fewer people from places like Haiti," that were  described with the word that I won't repeat again, and countries like Norway and Denmark and Sweden, as Justice Sotomayor suggested  earlier, that's very close to what we had in Arlington Heights itself.
So we do frame this as a race-based claim.
We do think it's racially motivated, particularly in light of the cross-cutting terminations we've seen.
As the district court  in our case put it, 13 up, 13 down, all non-white.
While  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So is  -- is that it? It's  --it's not Haiti particularly; it's all these countries have people of color as opposed to Denmark and Scandinavian  -- you know, Scandinavia generally and whatever?
Sure.
I certainly think that the record supports the idea that the President in particular has focused in on Haitians, but it is broader than that. Haitians are our plaintiffs.
But the relevant compare  --the relevant group here is  --is all TPS countries, all of which are non-white.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And -- and what if one thinks that -- you know, if -- you said there  was a determination that no matter what, there was going to be a change to Haiti's TPS status.
You know, there seems to have been a pretty clear determination that all TPS status should go, right?  There are no  --there's -- there's  --there's no TPS status that hasn't been renounced.
So how does that fact factor into this equal protection claim?
Sure.
Our position is is that you cannot have, for whatever reason, race-based or otherwise, a pre  -- a -- an agenda to end TPS because these are country-specific --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Quite  -- quite right. But that's a different kind of claim.
I  --I guess I'm just wondering, like, how to think  about the racial component of this if there seems to have been, you know, wherever and  whatever TPS I can find, it's not going to exist tomorrow.
I'm sorry, I'm not following.
Well, the race -based  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You know, that there's  -- you --you can -- you can argue that there was just like an across-the-board, we have to get rid of all these TPS, and the statutory requirements weren't followed and -- and  --and all of that, but  -- but the injection of this racial component into it, I guess I don't quite see how that operates when all of these programs went.
Well, again, I would point you back to both the President's statements and the Secretary's statements.

The  Secretary herself described people from Haiti and from 18 other all non-white countries as killers, leaches, entitlement junkies, saying  we don't want them, not one, while simultaneously enacting a policy, another humanitarian form of relief, for white and only  white South Africans.
So, if you want the comparator group, that's part of it.

And  --and it's true that the program, the refugee program under which the South  --the white South Africans were admitted is not TPS as such, but both statutes are  -- are motivated by the same policy from Congress  -- motivated by the same policy. They're both humanitarian programs.

In both TPS and with the special refugee program, it's the United States saying  these folks are facing some hardship in their home country, at least that's the stated basis, and we're going to let them in.

So it's -- it's not  --it's  -- it's the President's statements in which there is a comparator group, white versus  -- non-white countries versus white countries, and it's the fact that you've got the -- the -- that --those sort of sentiments being articulated into policy  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But more directly  --
-- with regard to South Africa.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- to Justice Kagan's point, isn't  --isn't your view that the reason why the President was saying all of  the TPS programs have to go is because the TPS program relates to countries that have large  minority or large racial compositions?
Yes, that's exactly right, Justice.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: In other words, the motivation for getting rid of all of them is that these programs "benefit" these kinds of people?
That  -- that -- yes, that's exactly right.
And I apologize if I  didn't follow that, but, yes, that is -- that is absolutely correct.
And under Arlington Heights, the  -- the racial motivation need be only one of many factors.
In every government policy I can  imagine, there is a facially legitimate reason given for the termination and the -- or for the government action.
The Arlington Heights  framework exists precisely for the purpose of sussing out whether impermissible racial considerations were part of  -- were -- were impermissibly in the mix.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But isn't it the case that TPS was terminated for quite a list of countries?  And I  --I -- I -- I can't seem to find the particular page of the transcript where the district court goes through them all.
And, yes, none of those is a Nordic country.
But -- and I don't like dividing up  the people of the world arbitrarily into three racial groups, but you -- you say they're all non-white and that's the -- that's the distinguishing characteristic?
That is the distinguishing characteristic that the district court held.
But I would  --I would emphasize, Justice Alito, that  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, do you think that if you put Syrians, Turks, Greeks, and other people who live around the Mediterranean  in a lineup, do you think you could say those people are -- are --that all of them, are they all non-white?
I understand that Syrians, I think, may be classified as white for purposes of the State Department.

I  -- or  -- or for under -- under certain government -- you know, certain government  programs, but, again, I think race is  --I think, you know, you'd have to poll the public to know what they think the race of a Syrian is.
I certainly think they're not white --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Poll the public?  Poll the American people?
Well  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Do they -- do they think Syrians are white?
I  --I'm -- I wouldn't think that most would, Justice Alito.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Really?
I really don't.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.
How about Turks?
I honestly haven't considered what racial component I would sort Turks into.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How about Greeks?
I  --I don't know the answer to that either.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How about southern Italians?  (Laughter.)

Well  -- well, certainly  --certainly, 120 years ago, when we had our last wave of European immigration, southern Italians were not considered white. So I think our concept of these things evolves over time.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How about Spaniards?
I think same answer. About 120 years ago, I don't think they were considered white.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You have a really large -- you have a really broad definition of who's white and who's not white.
As I said, I  don't like dividing the people of the world into these groups.
I  --I understand.

I  -- I would that say even under this Court's rationality jurisprudence, if you look at cases  like Moreno, it is not necessary for us to get strict scrutiny to win here because, irrespective of how you do the classification at issue here, under those courts' -- under those decisions  --excuse me, under those precedents, bare dislike of -- of an unpopular group is a sufficient basis to find that rational basis is not even satisfied.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Given your understanding of the review bar, wouldn't your APA arguments be exactly the same if there were no review bar?  In other words, what function does it  -- with respect to your APA arguments, in what way does the review bar restrict what you  -- what -- what you want to argue?

I will give the same answer that counsel for the Doe plaintiffs gave, which is that there are -- that  determination has the same meaning in the TPS statute that it had in the SAW statute at issue in the McNary case, that in that case, the antecedent obligations procedurally were  subject to judicial review even if the substantive determination was not.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: On that score, counsel, you agreed that the determination -- about the country conditions no longer meet the criteria is unreviewable?
Yes, the  -- the Secretary's substantive  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That final determination under, what is it, (B), right, (4)(B) -- (3)(B)?  Sorry.
That's unreviewable?
The Secretary's substantive conclusion as to the existence or non-existence  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, it's a determination, right?  I mean, that's what the statute says, right?
Correct.
And that's how we define determination.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.
And  -- and that takes effect once it's published in the Federal Register plus 60 days or something like that under -- under (3)(B), right?
That's correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.
And that's the determination and that's the effect of the  statute, but you say that a court can enjoin it anyway.
No, they can  -- well, for  -- we didn't get an injunction here.
We got 705 relief under the APA.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: 705 postponement.
Right.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, I mean, I'm  -- I'm just looking at what the court said.
I think, in the Syria case, it said the -- the  defendants' termination of TPS status for Syrians is hereby postponed.
And the D.C. Circuit in your case said the district court postponed termination, right?
That's correct.
That's Section 705 of the APA.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How is that not judicial review of the Secretary's determination?
Well, I would say that, again, the -- the claim --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I understand your process point, that you want to look at some antecedent things.
But how can it not be  judicial review of the determination if you're postponing the determination?
Because determination -- well, it  -- I --I can't -- it's difficult for me to answer that question without pointing out  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's difficult for me to answer the question too.
(Laughter.)
It's  -- well, no, the -- probably for different reasons, but the -- (Laughter.)

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, no, I don't know.
I'm asking  -- I'm --I'm just -- I am struggling with that.
No, I understand.
The question comes down to do you define  "determination" as coextensive with a broader term like "decision."  And we see --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, no, no.
I'm  -- I'm working within your framework for purposes of this question.

You know, (3)(B) says, once the Attorney General, but we all agree that's the Secretary, makes the determination the country conditions are no longer met, the  determination decision takes effect, published in the Federal Register, plus 60 days, something like that.
We -- we all agree on that.
And that  -- that's what the statute says about the effectiveness of the determination.
Right.
We have  -- we -- the  -- the final agency action here that was -- that was postponed is as counsel --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Is the determination.
It is the termination, not the determination, which is not subject to judicial review.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That  --that's what you got?
That is consistent with McNary.
It's consistent with Bowen.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Counsel, is your point that the -- that judicial review runs to the claim?  In other words, what -- what is happening in the judicial review bar, when it  says there's no judicial review, it means the court cannot consider the claim that's being  made, but that's different than what the court having considered the claim ultimately does?
Yeah.
That's exactly right.
And, again  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And so, at the end of the day, if the court considers a claim about a defect in the procedure and thinks it likely and, therefore, postpones the  termination while that claim is under review, that's not the same thing as reviewing the ultimate determination?

That's exactly right. The determination here has the same meaning that it had in McNary and Bowen, which is the substantive existence -- the existence substantively of the  --of the -- of the conditions for designation; i.e., is Haiti still safe?  The final agency action at issue here is the termination that was published in the Federal Register.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I -- I appreciate all of Justice Jackson's points and yours, but the statute says that determination is effective basically automatically, right, and it  -- it tells us when it's effective.
And it tells us how it's effective.
And that's what the statute -- that's what Congress told us, is once that determination is made, boom, it goes.

And -- and I -- I'm just struggling with how  --how that  --that could be true and  -- and yet it could also be true that -- that judicial review postponing that -- that termination decision is not judicial review of that judicial determination  -- of that determination.
Right.
Because the termination decision, the final agency action, includes substantially more than the  determination.
It includes things like when the  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It includes antecedent things, of course  --
Correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- that feed into that determination.
I  --I appreciate that. Okay.
All right.
Right.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Would you like to address  -- would you like to address the General's point, the Solicitor General's point, that this would drive a truck through the judicial review bar?
I don't think it would and no more so than, again, McNary or Bowen already did.
And -- and I would remind the Court that in Bowen and McNary -- excuse me, in McNary, the plaintiffs in that case won, and maybe this is responsive to Justice Gorsuch's  point.

Even though they were challenging the  procedure by which their SAW determinations was made, they still obtained injunctions and invalidation of the underlying determinations that they were challenging.
So this tension that we're identifying between the process and  the outcome is one that this Court has been -- and that the law has been comfortable with for over 30 years now.
As far as it driving a hole through the review bar, I would come back to the exact same point -- well, to a similar point, which  is the determination is -- is -- is off the table.
We agree with that.

Congress could not  have intended, we say, for the -- for things -- for these antecedent considerations not to be considered because, when it enacted the TPS statute, it already had the benefit of Bowen, and after it passed the review bar, Congress -- several years after it passed the review bar, Congress enacted IIRIRA, in which it -- it retained the language from Bowen -- from Bowen, from McNary.
So it's reasonable to read the  review bar in this case as consistent with that in Bowen and McNary.
In other words, Congress knows how to write broader language encompassing more than a specific determination.
It could write all  questions of law or fact.

And, in fact, in some other sections of Title VIII, it even writes language that we think would preclude procedure and process claims, like in  --in another section of Title VIII, it refers to all procedures and policies.
So Congress knows how to write broader language if it wants to, but it chose not to do so here, even within the background of Bowen and McNary.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Thomas, anything further?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How exactly does your equal protection argument work?  The Equal Protection Clause applies to states.
Well, this is a claim that arises under the Fifth Amendment -- the Fifth Amendment's equal protection guarantee.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Of life, liberty, and property?
That is the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment due process guarantee.
That's correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So how does it work?
Well, this Court has held repeatedly that  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No.
How does your claim work?  How do you get to the Fifth Amendment?
Because the Fifth Amendment constrains the federal government in the same way that the Fourteenth Amendment constrains states.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Alito, anything further?  Justice Sotomayor?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The Fifth Amendment says the federal government can't discriminate on the basis of race, correct?
That's exactly right. And  -- and the other thing I would -- I would emphasize that I was trying to get at earlier is that even under this case -- this Court's rationality cases, we still win.
Remember the -- the facts of Moreno. There was a facially plausible FDA program that  did not allow unmarried households to receive food stamps.
This Court nonetheless said that there was something else at play there, animus against a particular group, a bare dislike of a particular group.
And the President's statements, regardless of whether you consider them inherently racial or some other type of classification, reflect a bare dislike for Haitians in particular.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kagan, anything further?  Justice Gorsuch? Justice Kavanaugh? Justice Barrett? Justice Jackson? Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, General?
Very briefly, Mr. Chief Justice.

Congress balanced the risk that  -- by enacting a judicial review bar, Congress balanced the risk that there might be some decision that's erroneous or baseless or off-base against -- that would evade judicial review against the risk of what we're living through here, which is judicial micromanagement of the sorts of foreign-policy-laden determinations and decisions that are naturally conferred upon the  --the political branches. Justice Alito, turning to your "convoy of trucks" question, if you look at the briefing in this case, I think it vividly illustrates the  -- the concern that any exception that they put forth, and the exception morphs when they talk about it with different  --you know, different -- different formulations, any one of those exceptions creates a  --a -- an exception that would eviscerate the statutory  --or the judicial review bar here.

So, if you look, for example, at the Syria Respondents, the claims they raise, they raise the consultation claim, but as I pointed  out earlier, even those consultation claims are starting to bake in substantive criteria.
In other words, the district courts are saying,  well, you did consult, but your consultation wasn't thorough enough.
Therefore, we give you a D-plus.
Come back when you've got a B-minus consultation.
Maybe we'll let you terminate at that time.
And it gets even more striking when you get to their claims and things about the national interest criteria, which is unquestionably a substantive criteria.

And  then even further, if you look, for example, at the Syria Respondents, their pretext claim, they say, well, we're raising a pretext claim  and here's four reasons why we think this decision was pretextual.

Reason 3 is a long discussion of how they think the Secretary got  the administrative record wrong and made the wrong kinds of judgments and so forth. It gets even more striking when you read the Haiti Respondents' brief, where, in the 11 pages or so in which they discuss the -- the merits of their claims, by the second or third page, they've kind of abandoned any pretense that what they're raising is procedural, and they're raising the whole panoply of substantive challenge -- APA -type challenges to this particular decision.

So, to the extent there is a  -- you know, a  -- a -- a -- a judicial -- or any exception to the judicial review bar here, their own briefs, I think, demonstrate that  it's going to collapse under its own weight.
There's been reference to the presidential directives that we're supposed to provide.
There is a presidential directive that was provided.
It was provided in the executive order.
And the President directed  the Secretary to ensure that TPS designations are "appropriately limited in scope" and only as long as necessary to achieve the -- the textual directives in the statute.

And that is what the  -- that is what the Secretary did here. And then, Justice Gorsuch, as to your question, I do think it's helpful to end this case by look  -- or end this argument by looking at their prayer for relief in their complaints, which says we are challenging the termination decision as to these two  --these two countries.
We are saying that that termination  decision was unlawful.
It should be declared unlawful.
It should be set aside under the  APA.
It should be postponed under Section 705.
And I think, at that point, at a very high level, we are looking at a  --a request for judicial review of the termination determination, and that is exactly what the statute bars.
Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.
The case is submitted.
